customer_question: Why does the ICS Form show a yellow warning mark for this combination of referenced QDIDs, and what does it mean that 'this is acceptable via TCW (Test Case Waiver) application'?
question_variants: What causes inter-layer/intra-layer consistency check warnings when referencing older QDIDs?
What is a 'phantom inconsistency item' in the ICS consistency check?
How does a Test Case Waiver (TCW) resolve an ICS consistency check warning?
actual_issue: After Allion changed the registration's referenced component QDIDs to QDID:[ID] (LL/S140) and QDID:[ID] (Host/S140) and advanced to the review page, the customer noticed the ICS Form displayed a yellow warning mark for this QDID combination and asked why, and what 'acceptable via TCW (Test Case Waiver) application' meant. Allion explained that both referenced QDIDs were registered in 2019 under Bluetooth Core Specification v5.1, and at that time passed the intra-layer/inter-layer consistency checks against the ICS rules in effect then. However, for new registrations, the current ICS and consistency-check rules apply; as the specification has been updated, the ICS table structure has gained new items and corresponding new consistency-check rule conditions. When the new registration loads the referenced (2019-era) QDIDs' ICS information mapped onto the current ICS structure, the items that didn't exist in 2019 appear as blank, which the consistency-check engine interprets as 'Not Supported'. This caused 10 specific inter-layer rules (LL > GAP conditional-mandatory rules referencing GAP items 8/3, 8/4, 20/5, 20/6, 20/7 and CORE 40/3, mapping to LL items 3/1a, 3/4b, 3/5a) to be flagged as inconsistent, because LL items 3/1a, 3/4b, and 3/5a don't exist in QDID:[ID] (LL/S140)'s 2019-era ICS at all - making these 'phantom inconsistency items' that can be resolved by applying for a TCW (Test Case Waiver), which Allion stated would be applied and provided a reference URL for details.
plain_english_explanation: Bluetooth's registration system runs automated 'consistency checks' that verify a device's ICS (Implementation Conformance Statement) answers are logically consistent both within a single specification layer (intra-layer) and across layers (inter-layer, e.g., Link Layer vs. GAP). Component QDIDs registered years ago (e.g., 2019, under Core Spec v5.1) passed the consistency rules that existed at that time. But the Bluetooth specification and its ICS structure evolve - newer specs add new ICS items and new consistency-check rules that reference those items. When a new registration references an old QDID, the system maps that old QDID's ICS answers onto the current (expanded) ICS structure; any newly-added ICS items that simply didn't exist back when the old QDID was registered show up as blank/empty, and the consistency-check engine treats blank as 'Not Supported'. If a new consistency rule says 'if [some newer item] is Supported, then [some old-but-newly-required item] is Mandatory', but that 'old-but-newly-required item' didn't exist in the old QDID's ICS at all (so it's blank/'Not Supported'), the engine flags this as an inconsistency - even though it's really just an artifact of the ICS structure changing over time, not a real conformance problem. These are 'phantom inconsistency items'. A Test Case Waiver (TCW) is the mechanism to formally request that SIG accept the registration despite this kind of structural-mismatch warning, since it doesn't reflect an actual functional gap in the referenced component.
consultant_answer: The referenced QDID (LL/S140) and QDID (Host/S140) were registered in 2019 under spec v5.1, and naturally passed the intra-layer/inter-layer consistency checks in effect at that time. For a new registration, the currently-effective ICS and consistency-check rules apply; as the spec has been updated, new ICS table items and corresponding new consistency-check rule conditions have been added. So when the new registration loads the referenced QDIDs' 2019-era ICS information mapped onto the current ICS structure, items that didn't exist back then remain blank and are read by the consistency-check engine as 'Not Supported'. Specifically, in this registration, 10 LL>GAP conditional rules are flagged - the referenced LL items 3/1a, 3/5a, and 3/4b don't exist in the LL/S140 QDID's ICS at all, making these 'phantom inconsistency items', which can be resolved via TCW application to allow registration. Please see the attached URL for details.
decision_logic: When referencing older Component QDIDs (registered under an earlier Core Specification version) in a new registration, expect that the current (newer) ICS structure and consistency-check rules may flag inconsistencies for ICS items that didn't exist when the old QDID was registered - these blank/mapped-as-'Not Supported' items can trigger conditional-mandatory rules added in later spec versions. If the flagged items genuinely don't exist in the referenced QDID's original ICS (i.e., they are structural artifacts of spec evolution rather than real functional gaps), apply for a Test Case Waiver (TCW) to allow the registration to proceed despite the warning.
final_recommendation: When a registration referencing older Component QDIDs shows ICS Form consistency-check warnings, investigate whether the flagged items existed in the referenced QDID's ICS at its original registration time; if they are 'phantom' items introduced by later spec/ICS structure updates, apply for a TCW to resolve the warning and proceed with registration, and explain this distinction to the customer so they understand the warning doesn't indicate an actual functional deficiency.
risk_if_done_wrong: Misunderstanding an ICS consistency-check warning as an actual functional non-conformance (rather than a structural artifact of referencing an older QDID) could lead to unnecessary re-testing or registration delays. Conversely, failing to apply for a TCW when genuinely needed could block registration finalization entirely.
